d.x: England scored a goal at the death to even the score at one all.

death.e: From Middle English deth, deeth, from Old English dēaþ, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþu, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰówtus. More at die. Cognates Cognate with Scots daeth, daith, death, deeth, deith (“death”), North Frisian Duar, duas, düüs (“death”), Saterland Frisian Dood (“death”), West Frisian dea (“death”), Dutch dood (“death”), German Tod, Todt (“death”), Limburgish doead (“death”), Luxembourgish Doud (“death”), Yiddish טויט (toyt, “death”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål død (“death”), Faroese deyði (“death”), Icelandic dauði (“death”), Norwegian Nynorsk daude, død (“death”), Swedish död (“death”), Gothic 𐌳𐌰𐌿𐌸𐌿𐍃 (dauþus, “death”).

d.g: The bed on which someone dies.
d.x: He was once on his way to an old woman, who was on her death-bed and who had led a wicked life.

d.g: The last hours before death.
A grave; the site of a burial or entombment.
d.x: “Will you ask our oldest warriors to build me a barrow? Ask them to climb this headland and build me a death pile high on its top. Let my deathbed rise high above Hronesnesse.”

deathbed.e: From Middle English dethbed, from Old English dēaþbedd (“deathbed; grave”), equivalent to death + bed. Cognate with Swedish dödsbädd (“deathbed”). Compare also Dutch sterfbed (“deathbed”), German Sterbebett and Totenbett (both “deathbed”), Danish dødsleje (“deathbed”).

d.g: A strike or blow that leads to death, especially a coup de grâce.
d.x: He was also there at that fight when Hygelac folded under his deathblow.

d.g: Something that prevents the completion, or ends the existence, of a project etc.; a fatal setback.
d.x: The opening of the bridge dealt a deathblow to the ferry.

d.g: The number of deaths per given unit of population over a given period of time (usually per 1000 persons per year when not otherwise specified).
An extremely dangerous location, structure, or device.
d.x: Route 9 is a deathtrap; they should at least put up guard rails.

d.g: A plot device where a villain in a story puts a hero in an elaborate dangerous situation for the purposes of attempting a sadistic murder.

deathtrap.e: English death English trap English deathtrap From death + trap.

d.g: A vigil beside a dying person
One who guards a condemned person before execution.
A deathwatch beetle.
A debutante (a young woman who makes her first formal appearance in society).
d.x: Josie Powell that was, prettiest deb in Dublin. How time flies by!

d.g: A debutante ball or debut.
d.x: "When I met him at my deb, I fell for him. Wanted nothing more than to marry him. That it happened, even after all those years, felt as if the stars had finally aligned."

d.g: A female member of a gang.
d.x: Then one night Liz showed up at the factory with a scratched face and torn blouse. She had been in a fight at the park with another girl, a deb of the Porto Rican Flyers.

d.g: An event or enterprise that ends suddenly and disastrously, often with humiliating consequences.
d.x: The event proved to be a great debacle for the partisans of this prognosticator.

d.g: A breaking up of a natural dam, usually made of ice, by a river and the ensuing rush of water.
d.x: For several months after the debacle just described, the river Dranse, having no settled channel, shifted its position continually […]

debacle.e: From French débâcle, from débâcler (“to unbar; unleash”) from prefix dé- (“un-”) + bâcler (“to dash, bind, bar, block”) [perhaps from unattested Middle French and Old French *bâcler, *bacler (“to hold in place, prop a door or window open”)], from Vulgar Latin *bacculare, from Latin baculum (“rod, staff used for support”), from Proto-Indo-European *bak-. Also attested in Old French desbacler (“to clear a harbour by getting ships unloaded to make room for incoming ships with lading”) and in Occitan baclar (“to close”).

d.g: Disembarkation.
The act or an instance of debarring.

In the United States Food and Drugs Act, a penalty imposed on persons or companies that commit crimes in connection with applications for approval of drugs, in which such persons are barred from submitting or assisting in the submission of such an application.

debarment.e: English debar Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English debarment From debar + -ment.

d.g: The act of debasing or the state of being debased; a lowering or degradation, especially in character or quality.
d.x: She had given herself to Darrow, and concealed the episode from Owen Leath, with no more apparent sense of debasement than the vulgarest of adventuresses.

d.g: The lowering of the value of a currency by reducing the amount of valuable metal in the coins.

debasement.e: English debase Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English debasement From debase + -ment.

d.g: One who, or that which, debases.
d.x: […]a most jealous and barbarous governor, a debaser of the Roman empire, a corrupter of all that was good[…]

d.g: To participate in a debate; to dispute, argue, especially in a public arena.
d.x: "Debate me, coward!" snarled the completely normal intellectual.

d.g: To consider (to oneself), to think over, to attempt to decide
d.x: He was debating where he'd spend his holiday.

d.g: An argument, or discussion, usually in an ordered or formal setting, often with more than two people, generally ending with a vote or other decision.
d.x: After a four-hour debate, the committee voted to table the motion.

d.g: An informal and spirited but generally civil discussion of opposing views.
d.x: The debate over the age of the universe is thousands of years old.

debate.e: From Middle English debaten, from Old French debatre (“to fight, contend, debate, also literally to beat down”), from Romanic desbattere, from Latin dis- (“apart, in different directions”) + battuō (“to beat, to fence”).

d.g: One who debates or participates in a debate; one who argues.
d.x: William is a great debater.

debater.e: English debate Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English debater From debate + -er.

d.g: An individual act of debauchery.
d.x: Greene died of a debauch; and Marlowe, the gracer of tragedians, perished in an ignominious brawl.

d.g: An orgy.
d.x: The flowers, oppressive to the eyes, blazed with not a petal stirring, in a debauch of sun.

d.g: To morally corrupt (someone); to seduce.
d.x: But the Devil had met with too much Success in his first Attempts, not to go on with his general Resolution of debauching the Minds of Men, and bringing them off from God.

d.g: To debase (something); to lower the value of (something).
d.x: [S]aving of all kinds is pointless when interest is microscopic and state-sponsored inflation is debauching the currency.

debauch.e: 1590s, from Middle French desbaucher (“entice from work or duty”), from Old French desbauchier (“to lead astray”), from des- + bauch (“beam”), from Frankish *balkō, from Proto-Germanic *balkô, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, plank”); latter origin of balk. Evolution of sense unclear; may be literally “to shave/trim wood to make a beam” or may be “to leave/lure someone from a workshop”, Frankish *balkō perhaps also meaning “workshop”. Possible corruption by way of Anglicised French term bord (“edge, curb”): curb crawling as a synonym for prostitution. Parallels in modern German: Bordsteinschwalbe (“prostitute”, literally “Curb-stone-swallow”).

d.g: Somebody who is debauched; somebody who is dissolute and acts without moral restraint.
A person addicted to excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures.
Somebody who debauches or corrupts others; a seducer.

debaucher.e: English debauch Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English debaucher From debauch + -er.

d.g: An excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures; scandalous and immoral activities; involving sex, alcohol, or drugs without inhibition.
d.x: life of debauchery

debauchery.e: From debauch + -ery. First use appears c. 1642.

d.g: A certificate that certifies an amount of money owed to someone; a certificate of indebtedness.
d.x: This was the West Lancashire Railway, an ambitious but feckless little concern which, in a life lasting a quarter of a century, never earned a dividend, failed to keep up its debenture payments (despite a dangerous attempt to do so by issuing more debentures) and ended up in the hands of a receiver.

d.g: A type of debt instrument secured only by the general credit or promise to pay of the issuer, not involving any physical assets or collateral, now commonly issued by large, well established corporations with adequate credit ratings.
A document granting lenders a charge over a borrower’s physical assets, giving them a means to collect a debt, as part of a secured loan.

debenture.e: From earlier debentur, from Latin debentur (“they are owing”), supposedly the first word of such a document in early times. The ending was apparently influenced by words in -(t)ure.

d.g: The act or process of debilitating, or the condition of one who is debilitated; weakness.
A state of physical or mental weakness.
d.x: I was struck besides with the shocking expression of his face, with his remarkable combination of great muscular activity and great apparent debility of constitution

debility.e: From Middle English debylite, from Old French debilité (French débilité), from Latin dēbilitās (“weakness”), from dēbilis (“weak”), from dē- + habilis (“able”).

d.g: In bookkeeping, an entry in the left hand column of an account.
d.x: A cash sale is recorded as debit on the cash account and as credit on the sales account.

d.g: A sum of money taken out of a bank account. Thus called, because in bank's bookkeeping a cash withdrawal diminishes the amount of money held on the account, i.e. bank's debt to the customer.
To make an entry on the debit side of an account.
d.x: The economist also observed that some of the Victoria Line's cost should be debited to existing lines, as they would benefit from the rebuilding of their interchange stations with the new tube.

d.g: To record a receivable in the bookkeeping.
d.x: We shall debit your account for the amount of the purchase.

debit.e: Borrowed from Middle French debet, from Latin debitum (“what is owed, a debt”), neuter of debitus, past participle of debere (“to owe”); Doublet of debt.

d.g: A debtor

debitor.e: Borrowed from Latin debitor, equivalent to debit + -or. Doublet of debtor.

d.g: The removal of dead, damaged, or infected tissue to improve the healing potential of the remaining healthy tissue.
d.x: Originally, debridement of wounds was widely employed so that healing could occur as an acute wound instead of a chronic wound.

d.g: The removal of the dental tartar that has accumulated over teeth, typically done using hand tools and ultrasound instruments.
The act of debriefing, or the state of being debriefed.
The report of a mission or project, or the information so obtained.
present participle and gerund of debrief
Rubble, wreckage, scattered remains of something destroyed.
d.x: Melissa Foley clears debris in her neighborhood as the San Lorenzo River rises in Felton on Saturday, January 14.

d.g: Litter and discarded refuse.
Large rock fragments left by a melting glacier etc.

debris.e: Borrowed from French débris, itself from dé- (“de-”) + bris (“broken, crumbled”), or from Middle French debriser (“to break apart”), from Old French debrisier, itself from de- + brisier (“to break apart, shatter, bust”), from Frankish *bristijan, *bristan, *brestan (“to break violently, shatter, bust”), from Proto-Germanic *brestaną (“to break, burst”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrest- (“to separate, burst”). Cognate with Old High German bristan (“to break asunder, burst”), Old English berstan (“to break, shatter, burst”), German bersten (“to burst”). More at burst.

d.g: A debutante ball or debut.
d.x: 'I had my debs there,' she said, 'four years ago last summer.'

d.g: plural of deb

debs.e: Clipping of debutante or debut + -s (hypocoristic suffix).

d.g: An action, state of mind, or object one has an obligation to perform for another, adopt toward another, or give to another.
d.x: This long debt of confidence, due from me to him, whose bane and ruin I have been, shall at length be paid.

d.g: The state or condition of owing something to another.
d.x: I am in your debt.

d.g: Money that one person or entity owes or is required to pay to another, generally as a result of a loan or other financial transaction.
d.x: Bolsheviki had repudiated the four-billion-dollar debt which the government of the Tsar had contracted with the bankers.

d.g: An action at law to recover a certain specified sum of money alleged to be due

debt.e: From Middle English dette, dett, borrowed from Old French dete (French dette), from Medieval Latin dēbita, from Latin dēbitum (“what is owed, a debt, a duty”), neuter of dēbitus, perfect passive participle of dēbeō (“to owe”), contraction of *dehibeō (“I have from”), from de (“from”) + habeō (“to have”). Doublet of debit. Displaced native Old English eofot. The unpronounced "b" in the modern English spelling is a Latinisation from the Latin etymon dēbitum.

d.g: A person or firm that owes money; one in debt; one who owes a debt.
d.x: The debtor agreed to repay the loan within six months.

d.g: One who owes another anything, or is under obligation, arising from express agreement, implication of law, or principles of natural justice, to pay money or to fulfill some other obligation; in bankruptcy or similar proceedings, the person who is the subject of the proceeding.
d.x: As a debtor, he faced constant letters from the bank.

debtor.e: From Middle English dettour, from Old French detour, from Latin debitor, equivalent to debt + -or. Doublet of debitor. Displaced native Old English *sċola.

d.g: A computer program that helps the user to test and debug other programs, by enabling their step-by-step execution controlled by the user, setting of breakpoints, and monitoring values of variables.
d.x: 6. Memorandum PDP-23, ID Invisible Debugger, August 20, 1964.

d.g: present participle and gerund of debunk
The act of showing something to be false (or bunkum)
French composer who is said to have created Impressionism in music (1862-1918)
A performer's first performance to the public, in sport, the arts or some other area.
d.x: Hulking defenceman Gudbranson, who came to Vancouver in a trade with the Florida Panthers last May, scored in his debut for the Canucks.

d.g: The first public presentation of a theatrical play, motion picture, opera, musical composition, dance, or other performing arts piece.
d.x: Since making its debut two years ago, the program has gained cult status.

d.g: The first appearance of a debutante in society.
The coming-of-age celebration of a woman's eighteenth birthday.

debut.e: Borrowed from French début, from Middle French, derivative of débuter (“to move, begin”), from dé- + but (“mark, goal”), from Old French but (“aim, goal, end, target”), from Old French butte (“mound, knoll, target”), from Frankish *but (“stump, log”), or from Old Norse bútr (“log, stump, butt”); both from Proto-Germanic *butą (“end, piece”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewd- (“to beat, push”). Cognate with Old English butt (“tree stump”). More at butt. The Philippine sense is influenced by Spanish debut.

d.g: A young woman who makes her first formal appearance in society.
A female debutant, especially in sport and entertainment.

debutante.e: From French débutante. By surface analysis, debut + French -ante.

d.g: declared
Abbreviation of decrement.
Abbreviation of declaration.
Abbreviation of decoration.
A group, set, or series of ten , particularly
d.x: a decade of soldiers

d.g: A period of ten years , particularly such a period beginning with a year ending in 0 and ending with a year ending in 9.
d.x: The 1960s was a turbulent decade.

d.g: A period of ten days, particularly those in the ancient Egyptian, Coptic, and French Revolutionary calendars.
A series of prayers counted on a rosary, typically consisting of an Our Father, followed by ten Hail Marys, and concluding with a Glory Be and sometimes the Fatima Prayer.
A work in ten parts or books, particularly such divisions of Livy's History of Rome.

decade.e: From Middle English decade, from Old French decade, from Late Latin decādem (“(set of) ten”), from Ancient Greek δεκάς (dekás), from δέκα (déka, “ten”). In reference to a span of ten years, originally a clipping of the phrase decade of years. By surface analysis, dec- + -ade. Doublet of decad and dekad.

d.g: A state of moral or artistic decline or deterioration; decay
d.x: "Stability, however, is not enough. It leads too easily to stagnation, and thence to decadence."

d.g: The quality of being luxuriously self-indulgent.
d.x: the decadence of a five-star hotel

decadence.e: From French décadence, from Medieval Latin decadentia (“decay”), from *decadens (“decaying”), present participle of *decadere (“to decay”); see decay.

d.g: decadence.
The glucocorticoid drug dexamethasone
That has caffeine removed.
A decaffeinated coffee, tea, or soft drink.
A polygon with ten sides and ten angles.
An SI unit of mass equal to 10¹ grams. Symbol: dag
A ten-pointed star polygon.

decagram.e: From French décagramme. By surface analysis, deca- + gram.

d.g: A polyhedron with ten faces.
A design or picture produced in order to be transferred to another surface either permanently or temporarily.
A decorative sticker.
d.x: Decorating each alienation, each species of withdrawal, as cufflink, decal, aimless doodling, there was somehow always the post horn.

d.g: A texture overlaid on another texture to provide extra details.
To apply decals to.
The loss of calcium, as from the soil or from teeth or bones.

d.g: The process of transferring decorative designs onto surfaces using decals.
A decal.

decalcomania.e: French décalcomaniebor. English decalcomania Borrowed from French décalcomanie.

d.g: A decrease in temperature that occurs while heating metal through a range of temperatures in which change in structure occurs.
d.x: A very important feature is that steel containing hardening carbon, i.e., steel above the temperature of decalescence, is non-magnetic.

d.g: US spelling of decalitre.
Ten litres. Symbol: daL

decalitre.e: From French décalitre, equivalent to deca- + litre.

d.g: Alternative letter-case form of Decalogue.

decalogue.e: Borrowed from Middle French Décalogue, from Latin decalogus, from Ancient Greek δεκάλογος (dekálogos, from δέκα (déka, “ten”) + λόγος (lógos, “statement”)). Equivalent to deca- + -logue.

d.g: US spelling of decametre.

decameter.e: Borrowed from French décamètre. Equivalent to deca- + meter.

d.g: An SI unit of length equal to 10¹ metres. Symbol: dam
A unit of length equal to ten metres, also used as a poetic term for a line in a verse consisting of ten syllables or feet.

decametre.e: Borrowed from French décamètre. Equivalent to deca- + metre.

d.g: The act of decamping.
A prompt departure.

decampment.e: English decamp Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English decampment From decamp + -ment.

d.g: the act of decanting the supernatant liquid from a solid sediment
A vessel for decanting liquor.
A receptacle for decanted liquor, especially a crystal bottle with a stopper.
d.x: A decanter filled with smoke from smouldering incense.

decanter.e: English decant Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English decanter From decant + -er.

d.g: Beheading; the act of beheading or decapitating.

d.g: The ousting or destruction of the ruling body of a government or other organization.

d.g: The unseating of a senior politician.
d.x: The decapitation of the Foreign Secretary was a significant publicity coup for the opposition.

d.g: Having ten legs.
Any of various animals having ten legs or similar appendages, especially mollusks such as squid and cuttlefish.
Any crustacean of the order Decapoda, such as crabs or lobsters.
A nickname for either the 0-10-0 or 2-10-0 train configurations.
d.x: Naturally, odd pairs of engines and solitary examples lend themselves admirably to nicknames: for example, the Great Eastern 0-10-0 tank "Decapod", and the Lickey Incline banker, "Big Bertha", recently withdrawn from service.

decapod.e: Borrowed from French décapode. By surface analysis, deca- + -pod.

d.g: lobsters;  crayfish;  crabs;  shrimps;  prawns
scads especially mackerel scad;  cosmopolitan in distribution
Any enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of a carboxyl group, effectively removing carbon dioxide from a compound.
The removal of one or more carboxyl groups from a molecule
A verse form having ten syllables in each line.
An athletic contest consisting of ten events which includes sprinting, hurdling, jumping, and throwing over a span of two days.
d.x: He entered U.C.L.A. in 1954 and played for the renowned coach John Wooden’s basketball team there while training for decathlons.

d.g: A contest in science and math proving skill.

decathlon.e: From dec- + -athlon, coined for the 1912 Summer Olympics in analogy to the word pentathlon.

d.g: United States naval officer remembered for his heroic deeds (1779-1820)
Rot; any processes or result of organic matter being gradually decomposed, especially by microbial action.
d.x: tooth decay/dental decay—wood-decay fungi—bacterial decay—photochemical decay

d.g: Deterioration of condition; loss of status, quality, strength, or fortune.
d.x: civic and moral decay—systemic decay—fall into decay—urban decay—arrested decay—memory decay

d.g: Radioactive decay; decomposition of an atom or its nucleus.
d.x: alpha decay—gamma decay—fission decay—decay chain

d.g: Particle decay; decomposition of a sub-atomic particle.

decay.e: From Middle English decaien (“to decrease, diminish”) and decai (“deterioration, decline in value”), from Anglo-Norman decaeir (“to fall away, decay, decline”), from Vulgar Latin *dēcadere, etymologically restored form of Latin dēcidere (“to fall down, to fail, sink or perish”), from de- (“of, from, away, down”) + cadere (“to fall”). Compare decadent and decadence.

d.g: Death, departure from life.
d.x:
So should that beauty which you hold in lease
Find no determination: then you were
Yourself again after yourself's decease […]

d.g: To cause to die.

decease.e: From Old French deces (Modern French décès), from Latin dēcessus (“departure”).

d.g: A dead person.

d.g: Removing; departing; deceased.
d.x: satisfy every claimant upon the estate of a decedent person

decedent.e: From Latin decedens, present active participle of decedere (“to depart, die”).

d.g: An intentional action designed to mislead or deceive someone.
d.x: The whole conversation was merely a deceit.

d.g: The state of being deceitful or deceptive.
d.x: His mouth is full of curſing, and deceit, and fraud : vnder his tongue is miſchiefe and vanitie.

d.g: The tort or fraudulent representation of a material fact made with knowledge of its falsity, or recklessly, or without reasonable grounds for believing its truth and with intent to induce reliance on it; the plaintiff justifiably relies on the deception, to his injury.
the quality of being fraudulent

deceit.e: From Middle English deceyte, from Old French deceite, deçoite, from decevoir (“to deceive”), from Latin dēcipere (“to cheat, mislead”).

d.g: The state or quality of being deceitful; duplicity.
d.x: O full off all sutelte and disseytfulnes the chylde off the devyll, and the enemye of all righteousnes thou ceasest not to pervert the strayght wayes off the lorde.

deceitfulness.e: English deceitful Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English deceitfulness From deceitful + -ness.

d.g: A person who lies or deceives.

d.g: Another name for Satan.
someone who leads you to believe something that is not true

deceiver.e: Inherited from Middle English deceyvour, from Anglo-Norman decevour; by surface analysis, deceive + -er.

d.g: The act or process of decelerating.
d.x: The rocket is now in deceleration.

d.g: The amount by which a speed or velocity decreases (and so a scalar quantity or a vector quantity), an acceleration having a negative numerical value.

d.g: the last (12th) month of the year

december.e: From Middle English December, Decembre, from Old French decembre, from Latin december (“tenth month”), from Latin decem (“ten”); + Latin -ber, from -bris, an adjectival suffix; December was the tenth month in the Roman calendar.

d.g: The quality of being decent; propriety.

d.g: That which is proper or becoming.

decency.e: From Latin decentia, from decens. Equivalent to decent + -cy. Compare French décence.

d.g: Decennial: of or related to a ten-year period.
A decennium: a period of ten years.
Alternative form of decennial: relating to or denoting something that occurs every ten years, either in terms of numbers or as part of a tithing system.

decennary.e: From Latin decennis (“decennial, of ten years”) + -ary.

d.g: Synonym of decade: a ten year period.
d.x: G.B. still has to cope with the heritage of approx. 20 years of consecutive Conservative reigns, just as you guys are getting your act together after almost a decennium of Enlightened Ronnie.

decennium.e: From Latin decennium, from decennis (“10-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns), from deciēs (“ten times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives). Equivalent to decennial + -ium.

Alternative spelling of decentralization.

decentralisation.e: From French décentralisation, decentralise + -ation or de- + centralisation.

The state of being decentralized.

d.g: a misleading falsehood

demagnetization.e: From de- + magnetization or from demagnetize + -ation.

d.g: Alternative spelling of demagogue.
Alternative spelling of demagogue.
A political orator or leader, especially in a democratic system, who gains favor by pandering to or exciting the passions and prejudices of the audience rather than by using rational argument.
d.x: It is true that America has a paranoid streak in its politics, and demagogues come along from time to time to feed on anger and resentment.

d.g: A leader of the people.
To speak or act in the manner of a demagogue; to speak about (an issue) in the manner of a demagogue.
d.x: On the subject of foreign aid, although it is a relatively unimportant economic category, it is an area of expenditure that has frequently been demagogued and has been a favorite target of politicians during tough times in the domestic economy.

demagogue.e: From Middle French démagogue, from Ancient Greek δημαγωγός (dēmagōgós, “popular leader, mob leader”), from δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”). By surface analysis, dem- + -agogue.

d.g: The actions of a demagogue.
d.x: Long before the energy crisis the debate over deregulation of natural gas prices raged stormily, stirring high emotions, demagogueries and mutual deceptions, and with literally billions of dollars at stake.

d.g: Rhetoric that appeals to the prejudices of the people.

demagoguery.e: English demagogue Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -ārius Old French -ier Latin -ia Old French -ie Old French -eriebor. Middle English -erie English -ery English demagoguery From demagogue + -ery.

d.g: Rule by demagogue.
A polity ruled by a demagogue.
The quality of being a demagogue.
The actions of a demagogue.

demagogy.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δημαγωγία (dēmagōgía). By surface analysis, demagogue + y.

d.g: The desire to purchase goods and services.
d.x: Prices usually go up when demand exceeds supply.

d.g: The market force that causes buyers to be both willing and able to buy a good or service, as measured by the amount of that good or service that is currently salable at any given price point; the amount itself.
d.x: Supply and demand ebb and flow in a complex interplay.

d.g: A forceful claim for something.
d.x: Modern society is responding to women's demands for equality.

d.g: A requirement.
d.x: His job makes many demands on his time.

d.g: The act of marking off a boundary or setting a limit, notably by belligerents signing a treaty or ceasefire.
A limit thus fixed, in full demarcation line.
d.x: About sunset, he was leaning on the remains of an old wall, which had once probably surrounded a Roman encampment, and now served as a line of demarcation between two villages, as jealous of each other's claims as near neighbours usually are.

d.g: Any strictly defined separation.
d.x: There is an alleged, in fact somewhat artificial demarcation in the type of work done by members of different trade unions.

demarcation.e: First recorded c.1752, from Spanish línea de demarcación and/or Portuguese linha de demarcação, the demarcation line laid down by the Pope on May 4, 1493, dividing the New World between Spain and Portugal on a line 100 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. Both derive from demarcar, from de- + marcar (“to mark”), from Italian marcare, from the same Germanic root as march.

d.g: Alternative spelling of démarche.
family of imperfect mushrooms having dark-colored hyphae or conidia
an active volcano in northern Iran
The social, non-verbal behaviors (such as body language and facial expressions) that are characteristic of a person.
d.x: The man's demeanor made others suspicious of his intentions.

demeanor.e: From Middle English demenure, from the verb Middle English demenen, demeinen (“to handle, manage”), from Old French demener (“to guide, conduct”), from de- + mener (“to conduct, lead”), from Latin *mināre (“to drive”) and minor (“to project or jut forth”).

d.g: UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, and Commonwealth spelling of demeanor.
d.x: By some paradoxical evolution rancour and intolerance have been established in the vanguard of primitive Christianity. Mrs. Spoker, in common with many of the stricter disciples of righteousness, was as inclement in demeanour as she was cadaverous in aspect.

d.g: The quality of being demented.

A progressive decline in cognitive function due to damage or disease in the brain beyond what might be expected from normal aging. Areas particularly affected include memory, attention, judgement, language and problem solving.
d.x: In recent years some clinical trials involving potential dementia drugs have had disappointing setbacks.

d.g: Madness or insanity.

d.g: Alternative letter-case form of Demerara.

demerara.e: The placename derives from an Arawak word. Perhaps Malali ("fast running stream"), which would have originally been the name of a section of rapids, from which the Dutch called the whole river de Malali ("the Malali"), which (with incorporation of the definite article into the name, and alternation of l and r) became Demerara. Alternatively, perhaps Immenary or Dumaruni meaning “river of the letterwood”. The sugar is so-called because it was grown in the region around the river.

d.g: A quality of being inadequate; a disadvantage, a fault.
d.x: They see no merit or demerit in any man or any action.

d.g: A mark given for bad conduct to a person attending an educational institution or serving in the army.
That which one merits or deserves, either of good or ill; desert.
d.x: I fall to riſe, mount to thy maker, ſpirit, /. Leaue here thy body, death ha's her demerit.

demerit.e: From Middle English demerit, demerite, from Old French desmerite (modern French démérite) and its etymon Latin dēmeritum. By surface analysis, de- + merit.

d.g: a synthetic narcotic drug (trade name Demerol) used to treat pain
A lord's chief manor place, with that part of the lands belonging thereto which has not been granted out in tenancy; a house, and the land adjoining, kept for the proprietor's own use.
d.x: And whanne he sawe that he lete charce her oute of this land and bytoke hit me and alle this land in my demenys And when he saw that, he let chase her out of this land, and betook it me, and all this land in my demesnes.

d.g: A region or area; a domain.
d.x: Oft of one wide expanse had I been told / That deep-brow'd Homer ruled as his demesne; […]

demesne.e: From Middle English demayne, from Anglo-Norman demeyne, demene et al., Old French demeine, demaine, demeigne, domaine (“power”) (whence French domaine (“domain”)), a noun use of an adjective, from Latin dominicus (“belonging to a lord or master”), from dominus (“master, proprietor, owner”). See dame. Doublet of domain. The spelling with non-etymological s is partly due to influence from mesne and partly for the purpose of indicating a long vowel, as the s quiesced before a consonant; compare aisle, isle, Carlisle.

d.g: (Greek mythology) goddess of fertility and protector of marriage in ancient mythology;  counterpart of Roman Ceres
The goddess of the fertility of the Earth and harvests, protector of marriage and social order; daughter of Cronos and Rhea, mother to Persephone.

demeter.e: From Ancient Greek Δημήτηρ (Dēmḗtēr), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + μήτηρ (mḗtēr, “mother”).

d.g: son of Antigonus Cyclops and king of Macedonia;  he and his father were defeated at the battle of Ipsus (337-283 BC)

demetrius.e: From Ancient Greek Δημήτριος (Dēmḗtrios, literally “belonging to Δημήτηρ (Dēmḗtēr), the earth goddess”); from Δή (Dḗ), an early form of γῆ (gê, “earth”) + μήτηρ (mḗtēr, “mother”). Doublet of Dimitris and Dmitry.

d.g: A rich brown sauce in French cuisine, typically made from veal stock and espagnole sauce, used by itself or as a base for other sauces.

demiglace.e: French demi-glacebor. English demiglace Borrowed from French demi-glace.

d.g: A half-god or hero; the offspring of a deity and a mortal.
Someone held up for reverence as a supreme example.
d.x: "Ah! he is one of your idols, I suppose," said Lord Norbourne, with a slight approach to a sneer. "Youth is prone to admire; but it is odd how, in a few years, we discover the defects of our demigods...

demigod.e: From demi- + god. Calque of the Latin semideus (“half-god”), which is probably a coining by the Roman poet Ovid for less important gods such as dryads.

d.g: A large bottle with a short neck, sometimes with two small handles at the neck, sometimes encased in wickerwork.
d.x: “Reckon it's first-drink time,” the old prospector cried cheerily, and unearthed Monica's two-gallon demijohn.

demijohn.e: Partial calque of French dame-jeanne (literally “Lady Jane”), of uncertain origin. Note that the French Jeanne (“Jane, feminine of John”) has changed to the masculine form John, rather than the cognate English Jane.

d.g: United States film maker remembered for his extravagant and spectacular epic productions (1881-1959)

demille.e: Borrowed from Belgian French De Mille.

d.g: A sexually promiscuous woman (of the demimonde).

demimondaine.e: French demi-mondainebor. English demimondaine Borrowed from French demi-mondaine.

d.g: A class of women maintained by wealthy protectors; female courtesans or prostitutes as a group.
d.x: Skating Rinks are chiefly patronised by members of the demi[-]monde.

d.g: A group having little respect or reputation.
d.x: the literary demimonde

d.g: A member of such a class or group of persons.
d.x: On the evening of 4 August 1914 London's Café Royal was alive with its usual array of demimondes, dandies, aristocrats, émigrés, and self-styled bohemians.

demimonde.e: Borrowed from French demi-monde (literally “half-world”), from demi (“half”) + monde (“world; people”); possibly coined by French author and playwright Alexandre Dumas fils as the title of a comedic play, Le Demi Monde (1855): see the quotation from 1864.

d.g: Alternative spelling of demineralization.
The chemical engineering process in which mineral salts are removed from a liquid.
The loss of minerals, especially those of calcium, from bone.
The conveyance or transfer of an estate, either in fee for life or for years, most commonly the latter.
Transmission by formal act or conveyance to an heir or successor; transference; especially, the transfer or transmission of the crown or royal authority to a successor.
Death; decease.
d.x: Earth looked her loveliest to receive my sweet sister's gentle dust; but all was harsh and sullen as her own nature when Lady Avonleigh's haughty ashes returned to their original element. Immediately after her demise, her son went abroad, and I accompanied him.

d.g: The end of something, in a negative sense; downfall.
d.x: The lack of funding ultimately led to the project's demise.

demise.e: From Middle English demyse, dimise, dimisse, dymyse, from Middle French démise, the feminine singular past participle of démettre (“to put down, relinquish”); from Latin dēmissa, feminine singular of perfect passive participle of dēmittō. The "death" and "end" senses derive by way of euphemism from the legal sense, as a person's death was a common way that the legal demise could be accomplished. The verb is from Middle English dimisen, from the noun.

d.g: A thirty-second note, drawn as a crotchet with three tails.

d.g: The part of the ventilation system in a motor car that blows hot, dry air against the inside of the windscreen to prevent or remove condensation.
d.x: These screens incorporate a layer of transparent gold film in the laminations which forms an electric heating element to act as de-icer and de-mister.

d.g: Any of various devices that remove droplets of water from air.

demister.e: English demist Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English demister From demist + -er.

d.g: A small cup of strong black coffee.
d.x: He read old almanacs at the book-stalls on the quays, and he began to frequent another café, where more newspapers were taken and his post-prandial demi-tasse cost him a penny extra, and where he used to con the tattered sheets for curious anecdotes, freaks of nature, and strange coincidences.

d.g: The cup in which this coffee is served.

demitasse.e: From French demi-tasse (literally “half cup”), from demi- (“half-”) + tasse (“cup”).

d.g: The (usually benevolent) being that created the universe out of primal matter.
d.x: A demiurge or craftsman god takes pre-existing matter and fashions it in light of the eternal Forms.

d.g: A (usually jealous or outright malevolent) being who is inferior to the supreme being, and sometimes seen as the creator of evil.
d.x: This was the earnest attempt of a Christian to explain in some detail how God might act using natural law, although his critics noted that such a Creator had more in common with a gnostic demiurge than the transcendent God of the Judeo-Christian tradition.

d.g: Something (such as an idea, individual or institution) conceived as an autonomous creative force or decisive power.
d.x: An abiding tradition depicted the sage-kings of yore as demiurges who invented useful technologies to advance the progress of civilization. For example, Shun was acclaimed by the philosopher Mozi (circa late fifth century BCE) for teaching farming, pottery, and fishing to his subjects.

d.g: The title of a magistrate in a number of states of Ancient Greece, and in the city states (poleis) of the Achaean League.

demiurge.e: From Ancient Greek δημιουργός (dēmiourgós, “one who works for the people; a skilled workman, a handicraftsman”) (whence Latin dēmiūrgus, French démiurge), from δήμιος (dḗmios, “belonging to the people, public”) (from δῆμος (dêmos, “the people”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂mos (“people”), from *deh₂- (“to divide”) + Ancient Greek -ιος (-ios), from Proto-Indo-European *-yós (suffix creating an adjective from a noun)) + Ancient Greek -ουργός (-ourgós, “worker”) (from ἔργον (érgon, “labour; task; work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom (“work”)). No relation with English demi- (as in demigod).

d.g: A demonstration or visual explanation.
d.x: The professor prepared a demo to help her class understand the topic.

d.g: A recording of a song meant to demonstrate its overall sound for the purpose of getting it published or recorded more fully.
d.x: After hearing the demo, the record label approved funding to record the song with a full band.

d.g: An example of a product used for demonstration and then sold at a discount.
A march or gathering to make a political protest.
d.x: Elli standing there, takes a sip of her tea, fixes hostile eyes on Somraj and says, ‘Well, what are you waiting for? You signed the petition against yourself, will you now join our demo against you?’

d.g: An edition of limited functionality to give the user an example of how the program works.
d.x: The game's developers released a demo version to the public 3 months before the full release.

d.g: A non-interactive audiovisual computer program developed by enthusiasts to demonstrate the capabilities of the machine. See demoscene.
d.x: Effect 6: Gouraud spacecut - Probably the worst effect in the demo - has been done miles better before!

d.g: A democrat.
A demographic group.
d.x: No more ‘is it good?’ or even ‘is it original?’, only ‘does it work in the demo?’ – ‘demo’ as in ‘demographics’, not to be confused with ‘democracy’, much less ‘demonstration’.

demo.e: Clipping of demonstration and various other words beginning with "demo-". Clipping of demonstrate. Clipping of demolish.

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of demobilization.
d.x: Army railwaymen from an H.Q. in Switzerland controlled demobilisation traffic all over Europe, including the famous MEDLOC train service.

d.g: The disorganization or disarming of troops which have previously been mobilized or called into active service; the change from a war footing to a peace footing; the act of demobilizing.
Rule by the people, especially as a form of government; either directly or through elected representatives (representative democracy).
d.x: Everyone who wanted to speak did so. It was democracy in its purest form.

d.g: A government under the direct or representative rule of the people of its jurisdiction.
d.x: Since the wisest and most moral would not necessarily be the choice of the majority of people, Plato's Republic is not a democracy.

d.g: A state with a democratic system of government.
d.x: After almost four decades of authoritarian rule, South Africa became a democracy in April 1994.

d.g: Belief in political freedom and equality; the "spirit of democracy".
d.x: As states of the human spirit democracy, righteousness, and faith have much in common and may be cultivated by the same means...

democracy.e: From Middle French democratie (French démocratie), from Medieval Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā). By surface analysis, demo- (“people”) + -cracy (“rule”).

d.g: A supporter of democracy; an advocate of democratic politics (originally (historical) as opposed to the aristocrats in Revolutionary France).
d.x: The democrats now have majority control in almost all areas except the Islands District Council, where they won seven seats, and the pro-Beijing camp obtained 11 seats.

d.g: Someone who rules a representative democracy.
A large light uncovered wagon with two or more seats.

democrat.e: From French démocrate, from démocratie (modelled on aristocrate (“aristocrat”)), equivalent to demo- + -crat.

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of democratization.
d.x: Five years later, when the institute published its first dataset of global democracy, its experts realised that things were rapidly going in the wrong direction. “Now, all of us researching democratisation have become researchers on autocratisation,” Lindberg says.

d.g: The introduction of democracy, its functions or principles, to an area or country which did not have democracy previously.
The spread of democracy as a concept.
The making more democratic of a political system.
d.x: Autocratization is more prevalent than democratization in every region of the world.

d.g: The broadening of access to something, especially for the sake of egalitarianism.
Greek philosopher who developed an atomistic theory of matter (460-370 BC)
The inverse of the effect of modulation, or applying a signal to a carrier.
d.x: A radio transmitter applies modulation to a carrier wave and the receiver applies demodulation to it to recover the message.

d.g: Any device that demodulates a signal

demodulator.e: English demodulate English -or English demodulator From demodulate + -or.

d.g: (Greek mythology) a mysterious and terrifying deity of the underworld

demogorgon.e: Pseudo-loan from Ancient Greek, most likely actually invented by a Christian scholar c. 350–400 C.E. The origins of the name are uncertain, partly because the figure itself was possibly of imaginary coinage. Various theories suggest that the name is derived from the Greek words daemon (“spirit”, given the Christian connotations of “demon” in the early Middle Ages)—or, less likely demos (“people”)—and Gorgon or γοργός (gorgós, “grim”). A less accepted theory claims that it is derived from a variation of “demiurge”.

d.g: A person who studies demography.
a scientist who studies the growth and density of populations and their vital statistics
The study of the characteristics of human populations, especially with regards to their makeup and fluctuations and the social causes behind these.
The study of the structure and population dynamics of other lifeforms, such as mammals, insects, plants, etc.
The particular demographic makeup of a population.
d.x: the schoolʼs demography began to change with the immigrants and their offspring pouring in

demography.e: From demo- (“people”) + -graphy (“written representation of”) (From Ancient Greek δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) and Ancient Greek -γραφία (-graphía), from γραφή (graphḗ, “writing, drawing, description”)).

d.g: A damselfly of the family Calopterygidae.
A young lady; a damsel; a lady's maid.
The Numidian crane (Grus virgo).

demoiselle.e: Borrowed from French demoiselle. The bird is so called on account of the grace and symmetry of its form and movements. Doublet of damsel, doncella, and donzella.

d.g: present participle and gerund of demolish
The process of demolishing or destroying buildings or other structures.
d.x: At Kiwi, 40 miles from Nelson [New Zealand], eight women installed themselves in the goods shed, taking with them their knitting, and a supply of food and magazines. The demolition crew was unable to pull the building down without injuring them.

demolition.e: From Old French demolition, from Latin dēmōlītiō (“a tearing down”). Equivalent to demolish + -ion.

d.g: An evil being resident in or working for Hell; a devil.
A false god or idol; a Satanic divinity.
A very wicked or malevolent person; also (in weakened sense) a mischievous person, especially a child.
A source (especially personified) of great evil or wickedness; a destructive feeling or character flaw.
d.x: The demon of stupidity haunts me whenever I open my mouth.

d.g: A tutelary deity or spirit intermediate between the major Olympian gods and mankind, especially a deified hero or the entity which supposedly guided Socrates, telling him what not to do.

demon.e: From Middle English demon, a borrowing from Medieval Latin dēmōn, daemōn (“lar, familiar spirit, guardian spirit”), from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “dispenser, god, protective spirit”). Displaced native Old English sċucca and Old English þyrs. Doublet of daimon.

d.g: Alternative form of demonetization.
The act or process of demonetizing (withdrawing as legal tender).

d.g: The act or process of demonetizing (making content ineligible to earn money).
Alternative spelling of demonization.
d.x: Each side's current demonisation of the other generates heat rather than light, and pushes a settlement further away.

d.g: Belief in, or worship of demons or devils.
d.x: It is very much to be doubted if Mervyn Hogarth had ever in his life given more than a passing thought to any black art or occult science. Certainly he was innocent of prolonged interest in, let alone any practice of, diabolism, witchcraft, demonism, or such cult.

d.g: The quality of being demonic.
d.x: What significant illustration of the demonism of the wind does a fallen palm present!

d.g: An act or event attributed to demons or devils; an evil act.
d.x: So many boys, so many places have disappeared. Blue Gate Fields, scene of many an Asiatic demonism, is gone.

d.g: The act of demonizing.
Something demonized.
Worship of demons.

demonolatry.e: From Latin daemonolatria. By surface analysis, demono- + -latry.

d.g: The quality of being demonstrable.
The act of demonstrating; showing or explaining something.
A prisoner's act of beating up another prisoner.
An event at which something will be demonstrated.
d.x: I have to give a demonstration to the class tomorrow, and I'm ill-prepared.

d.g: Expression of one's feelings by outward signs.
A proof.
d.x: He read the proposition. […] So he reads the demonstration of it, which referred him back to such a proposition,; which proposition he read.

demonstration.e: From Middle English demonstracioun, from Old French demonstration, from Latin dēmōnstrātiōnem, from dēmōnstrāre (“show or explain”), from dē- (“of or concerning”) + mōnstrāre (“show”). Morphologically demonstrate + -ion.

d.g: The state or quality of being demonstrative.

The act of corrupting or subverting morale, discipline, courage, hope, etc., or the state of being corrupted or subverted in morale.
d.x: the demoralization of an army or navy

d.g: The act degrading the moral value of something.

d.g: To submit a demurrer (“motion by a party to a legal action for the immediate or summary judgment of the court on the question of whether, assuming the truth of the matter alleged by the opposite party, it is sufficient in law to sustain the action or defence, and hence whether the party bringing the motion is required to answer or proceed further”).
d.x: He that demurreth in Law confeſſeth all ſuch matters of fact as are well and ſufficiently pleaded.

Dear John letter.e: While the exact origins of the phrase are unknown, it is commonly believed to have been invented by Americans during World War II. Large numbers of American troops were stationed overseas for many months or years, and as time passed many of their wives or girlfriends decided to begin a relationship with a new man rather than wait for their former one to return. As letters to servicemen from wives or girlfriends back home would typically contain affectionate language, a serviceman receiving a note beginning with a curt "Dear John" (as opposed to the expected "Dear Johnny", "My dearest John" or simply "Darling" for example) would instantly be aware of the letter's purpose.
